he journey was like a strange, tormented dream. They travelled

eight hundred miles in three weeks. They left Georgia following
the spectacular Appalachian Mountains and continued through the
Confederate states of Alabama, Mississippi and Arkansas and into the
Union state of Missouri with its vast forests. A memorable moment
was crossing the majestic Mississippi River, but the devastating
effects of the war were everywhere and impossible to forget — towns
in ruins, plantations destroyed, thousands of men in grey or blue uni-
forms, many of them mutilated by terrible weapons of destruction,
and piles of coffins waiting for the dead.
The stagecoach wasn’t comfortable, but they stopped at night to
sleep. During the day nobody talked much; the war made everyone
sad and silent. They often heard a familiar name, Lincoln, pronounced
with respect and hope. The other five passengers in the stagecoach

changed frequently. One day another passenger, a plantation owner

from Alabama, spoke to Dinah.
“Girl, you had a job, a home and food. Now what have you got?”

The Native Americans

n the 1600s, after the European colonisation of America,

the Native Americans abandoned their agricultural life and

became nomadic hunters. This change was possible thanks
to the presence of wild horses and their ability as riders. Now, more
than ever, their lives depended on the calendar of Nature, following the
migrations of the buffalo. They lived in harmony with Nature, with no
concept of private property. The Indians of the plains believed that
Wakan Tanka was the creator of the world, and that when they died
they went to the Happy Hunting Ground. The stories and legends of
the tribe were recorded in oral traditions, often by the Shaman, their
spiritual leader and “Medicine Man”. Political decisions were made by
a tribal council of men, but equality was important and women were
respected; they had a precise role, the preparation of food and clothes,
while the men hunted and prepared weapons. Children were also very
important and were given a name at the age of eight or nine, when they
had their first “vision”, usually of an animal. Their education came from
their uncle, their mother’s brother. Generally, a family consisted of three
or four children, and tribes were divided into bands with family connections.
It was a harmonious society. Until the arrival of the white man, there
was no word for law in the Indian vocabulary.

What an adventure! Matt and I time-tripped to America to
rescue Mr Wells. We met Dinah, a slave / master in Atlanta
— then we went to Kansas with tickets that Matt won because
he made a bad / great shot at billiards. We saw the awful /
safe effects of the Civil War. We stopped at Fort Laramie and
met braves /soldiers. Then we met some real American
Indians / Redskins. We stayed in their camp and discovered
Mr Wells was there too, in a tepee / cabin. The Indians have
a lot of traditional rights / rites, including the Sundance /
Happy Hunting Ground. We also went to Sand Creek,
where there was a treaty / massacre. We escaped just in time.
We're safe but we lose / miss our friends from the past
(especially Johnny).
